preamble: Excrescent [t] appears after /s/ or /n/, usually at the end of a word. A transitional stop between a nasal or sibilant and silence (or a following consonant) gets reanalysed as a full segment. English added it to adverbs in -s around 1350 (against, amongst, whilst, amidst), and it shows up synchronically in /ns/ clusters (prince [prɪnts], making it sound like prints). Middle and Early New High German added the same t after s in several nouns (MHG obeȥ > Obst, ackes > Axt, bābes > Papst, palas > Palast), and Dutch did so after s and ch (Middle Dutch rijs > rijst, huls > hulst, burch > burcht).

examples.note: The parasitic -t was added around 1350, probably helped by confusion with the superlative ending -est.
among + adverbial genitive -s, followed by an excrescent -t. Whilst (< whiles) and amidst (< amids) arose the same way.
Synchronic stop epenthesis in /ns/: the velum closes before oral release, which creates a transitional [t]. Many speakers merge prince with prints and sense with cents.

examples.from: Middle High German obeȥ (Old High German obaȥ) 'fruit'
examples.note: Excrescent dental after s, as in Axt and Papst.
Late MHG already shows axt and pābest, bābest, alongside the older forms without -t.
MHG palast was attested beside the more usual palas.

examples.from: Middle Dutch rijs 'rice' (< Old French ris)
Middle Dutch croos 'offspring' (< Old French croist)

examples.note: Paragogic -t after a word-final fricative; the older form survives as burg.
